newsitem.title: HONG KONG: New Hong Kong honours to reward pro-China loyalty.
newsitem.headline: New Hong Kong honours to reward pro-China loyalty.

text.p: Just days before China takes over, Hong Kong's future leader Tung Chee-hwa set up a system of honours on Wednesday to reward those who helped smooth the way.

As a rival to such insignia as Queen Elizabeth's Birthday Honours and the onetime Soviet Order of Lenin, Tung's office created the "Grand Bauhinia Medal", named after the blossom to be Hong Kong's emblem after the colonial British withdraw in six days time.

China's Foreign Minister Qian Qichen will hand out the first batch of 12 medals next Wednesday in Government House, the seat of the colonial Governor Chris Patten, who is leaving town at the stroke of midnight on June 30.
The move comes just a week after Britain showered its Hong Kong stalwarts, such as Financial Secretary Donald Tsang, with knighthoods and other awards for their loyal public service.
"The awards have been instituted in order to give due recognition to contributions to the reunification with China," Tung's office said in the announcement.
The achievers to be "knighted" under the new China-backed Hong Kong awards include members of committees which have crafted the new power structures to replace the colonial order.
Qian, accompanying President Jiang Zemin here for the grand handover ceremony, will hand out the awards in the colonial mansion.

The irony will be profound -- it will be just four days after heir to the British throne Prince Charles hands out the knighthoods in the same grand edifice at a traditional British investiture ceremony.

Those honoured, by Tung's announced criteria, will all be people who have "fostered among Hong Kong people a love for the Motherland", "showed concern and support and identified with China's achievements", and "made an outstanding contribution to the Hong Kong community".
The awards will become an annual event every July 1, the day that China recovers from Britain the territory it lost in the 19th century opium wars.

One of the rewarded dozen is Elsie Tu, an 84-year-old Englishwoman from Newcastle Upon Tyne who has crusaded for the underdog in colonial Hong Kong for five decades and is the sole white face on a new legislature China plans to install here.

Also honoured are Lo Tak-shing and Simon Li, the former an entrepreneur-politician and the latter a judge turned power seeker who both ran in a contest last December to be China's man in Hong Kong -- a battle won by Tung.

Lo and Li, both fairly pro-China in their statements, provided an appearance of plurality in a competition which most observers believed had been sealed in a golden handshake Tung received from Jiang in Beijing in January last year.

The new award will also go to Henry Fok Ying Tung, a powerful tycoon who helped China overcome trade-embargo difficulties during the Korean War and is widely regarded as a kingmaker in Hong Kong, and a strong backer of shipping magnate Tung.
Xu Simin, a left-wing publisher and doyen of the pro-Beijing camp in Hong Kong, will also receive the medal, based on one of Hong Kong's most common flowers, also known as the tree orchid.
